feature.imageCaption: The bucket, the tiara, and the last movie of the season
feature.title: "Carrie" closes the outdoor movie season on the Ijams Park lawn
feature.deck: The last Movies Under the Stars of the year is the original prom-night horror, fifty years old this fall, shown outdoors on the first Friday of October with the woods right behind the screen.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Fri Oct 2 · doors 6 PM · movie at dark, about 7:30

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Visitor Center lawn, Ijams Park · 2915 Island Home Ave

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $12 · members of Ijams Park or Central Cinema get a discount code by phone

facts.label: The film
facts.value: "Carrie" (1976) · directed by Brian De Palma · Sissy Spacek · 98 minutes

facts.label: Food & drink
facts.value: Food trucks and the Ijams beer garden · no coolers, no outside alcohol

facts.label: Weather
facts.value: Mostly sunny and 89 on Friday · a 30% chance of a shower from mid-afternoon into the evening

body.text: Ijams Park and Central Cinema have been showing movies on the Visitor Center lawn since spring, and Friday is the last one of the season. They saved the right film for October: the original "Carrie," Brian De Palma's 1976 adaptation of the first novel Stephen King ever published, with Sissy Spacek as the girl nobody at school should have pushed that far. It came out in November 1976, which makes it fifty years old this fall.
Why outdoors is the way to see it

A horror movie plays differently with no walls. The screen goes up on the lawn, the sun sets at 7:18, and by the time the prom scene arrives the only light for a quarter mile is the one on the screen, with the tree line sitting dark behind it. The film runs 98 minutes, so a 7:30 start has everyone walking back to the car a little after nine. It is an R-rated movie, and the park allows dogs on a leash, so plan the rest of the household accordingly.
The practical part

Doors open at six, and the hour and a half before dark is for dinner: food trucks are on the property and the Ijams beer garden is open. Coolers and outside alcohol stay home. Bring a lawn chair or a blanket. Tickets are $12 a person, and members of either Ijams Park or Central Cinema can call (865) 577-4717, extension 1001, for a discount code. Friday is 89 and mostly sunny with a 30 percent chance of a shower after two o'clock and into the evening, so check the event page before you load the chairs.

stories.label: Ijams Park
stories.title: A starlight paddle goes out on a moonless river Friday night
stories.deck: The moon doesn't rise until 11:41 Friday night, so the two hours Ijams Park naturalists spend on the Tennessee River after sunset belong to the stars, clouds permitting.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Ijams River Landing · 3507 Island Home Pike

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $45 · kayak, life vest and headlamp included

facts.label: Ages
facts.value: 14 and up · under 18 with an adult

facts.label: Weather
facts.value: Mostly cloudy Friday night · 30% chance of a shower · low 66

facts.label: Waiver
facts.value: One adventure release per calendar year

facts.label: More dates
facts.value: Oct 16 · Oct 17 · Oct 30 · all at 7 PM

body.text: Last week the park paddled under a full Harvest Moon. This week it does the opposite. Friday's Starlight Paddle leaves the River Landing on Island Home Pike at seven, eighteen minutes before sunset, and the moon does not come up until 11:41 that night, so once the light is gone the river is as dark as it gets this close to a city. Ijams Park naturalists lead the two hours and talk through what lives along the bank after dark and what is overhead.
What the forecast says

The sky is the open question. Friday night is forecast mostly cloudy with a 30 percent chance of a shower and a low of 66, which is warm for October and comfortable on the water. If the clouds win, the river at night is still the river at night, and the same paddle runs again October 16, 17 and 30.
The practical part

Forty-five dollars covers the kayak, the life vest and a headlamp. It is built for ages fourteen and up, and anyone under eighteen comes with an adult. Bring water and clothes you can paddle in. Everyone signs the adventure release once a year if they haven't already. Register ahead rather than driving down.

stories.label: Kern's
stories.imageCaption: Painted to look like it's hanging off the brick
stories.title: Giant fishing lures hang down the Kern's tower, painted for the SoKno Art Walk
stories.deck: A muralist has turned the old bakery's tower into a tackle box several stories tall. It is one of the first pieces of a rail trail that will run from Chapman Highway to Ijams Park.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: The tower at Kern's · 2201 Kern's Rising Way

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: Free · it's on the outside of the building

facts.label: The trail
facts.value: SoKno Rail Trail & Art Walk · 3.8 miles, Chapman Highway to Ijams Park · scheduled to open this fall

facts.label: The art walk
facts.value: 1.5 miles, Chapman Highway to Island Home · four murals and four sculptures to start

facts.label: Paid for by
facts.value: A $1 million gift from the Lawson Family Foundation

facts.label: Who
facts.value: Legacy Parks Foundation, with Gulf & Ohio Railway, the City of Knoxville and Dogwood Arts

facts.label: Coming next
facts.value: A painted train engine, and ten-foot letters spelling SOKNO

body.text: Look up the next time you are at Kern's. The tower on the old bakery now carries "Shiny Objects," a mural of fishing lures blown up to the size of the building, painted with hard cast shadows so they appear to dangle off the brick. The artist is Naomi Haverland, who works out of Florida and painted one of the KnoxWalls murals at Emory Place in 2024. She has said she picked lures because they are built to catch the eye and because fishing is part of life in East Tennessee.
What it belongs to

The mural is one of four planned for the SoKno Rail Trail & Art Walk, a 3.8-mile trail on the old rail line from Chapman Highway to Ijams Park. The first mile and a half, from Chapman Highway to Island Home, is the art walk, and it opens with four murals and four sculptures chosen with Dogwood Arts and paid for by a million-dollar gift from the Lawson Family Foundation. Legacy Parks Foundation told its annual luncheon on September 25 that the mural at Kern's is finished, that another was days from starting, and that more pieces go in over the next few weeks. The trail is scheduled to open this fall.
What comes next

Two more pieces have been announced: a historic train engine that will be set on the trail and painted, and a set of ten-foot metal letters spelling SOKNO, each one a mural. Legacy Parks is raising $25,000 for the letters, and a single letter can be sponsored for $5,000. The lures, meanwhile, cost nothing to look at. Kern's is open seven in the morning to ten at night Thursday, to eleven Friday, eight to eleven Saturday and nine to nine Sunday.

stories.deck: The sports grill on Mimosa Avenue serves brunch nine to two both weekend days with every screen on. Saturday's 3:30 kickoff means there is time to eat first and settle in.

facts.label: Brunch
facts.value: Sat and Sun · 9 AM – 2 PM · every screen on

facts.label: Pucker Hour
facts.value: Mon–Fri 5–6 PM · $1 Pucker Lager, $3 wells and prosecco

body.text: Puckers keeps weekend brunch on the menu from nine to two on Saturday and Sunday, and this Saturday the schedule is kind to it. Tennessee hosts Auburn at 3:30, so the kitchen's brunch service ends an hour and a half before kickoff instead of colliding with it the way last week's noon game did. The room bills itself as a game-day headquarters, with the screens on for Vols Saturdays and NFL Sundays alike.
How the day works

A mid-afternoon kickoff fills a sports bar across the river from the stadium well before the game, so a late brunch is the way to already have a seat when it starts. Parking is the garage behind the building, and the room takes reservations. Sunday runs the same brunch hours, with the Titans away at Baltimore at one.

stories.label: Urban Wilderness
stories.title: Volunteers dig in at Baker Creek on Saturday to get the trails ready for Fall Fest
stories.deck: The mountain bike club's monthly work party is open to anyone with gloves and sturdy shoes. Three hours of trail repair and pulling invasive plants, and then the sponsors buy lunch.

facts.label: Bring
facts.value: Sturdy shoes, gloves, safety glasses, water

facts.label: Provided
facts.value: Tools · lunch at noon from Bear Paw Bikes and 71 South · cold drinks from Creature Comforts

facts.label: With
facts.value: Trees Knoxville, leading the invasive-plant removal

facts.label: Weather
facts.value: Mostly cloudy · 50% chance of showers · high 84

body.text: The trails at Baker Creek do not maintain themselves. The Appalachian Mountain Bike Club holds a work party on the first Saturday morning of most months, and October's is at Baker Creek Preserve, where the job is getting the trails in shape for the club's Fall Fest on November 6 and 7. Trees Knoxville is joining to lead the removal of invasive plants alongside the trail work.
Who can come

Anyone. You do not need to ride a bike, belong to the club or sign up ahead; the club calls these the best chance for trail users of every kind to give a morning back. It supplies the tools. You bring sturdy shoes, gloves, safety glasses and water, and you sign the club's 2026 waiver if you haven't. Families with kids are welcome.
The practical part

Work runs nine to noon, and at noon Bear Paw Bikes and 71 South provide lunch, with cold drinks from Creature Comforts. Saturday is mostly cloudy with a high of 84 and a 50 percent chance of showers, so dress for mud. The preserve is at 1516 Taylor Road.

stories.label: Ijams Park
stories.title: The moss walk at Mead's Quarry goes out Saturday, the last one on the calendar
stories.deck: Most people stopped looking closely at moss around age seven. An Ijams Park naturalist spends two hours at the quarry on how to tell the species apart and what they do for the woods.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Mead's Quarry · 3526 Island Home Ave · meet staff at the picnic tables

facts.label: Weather
facts.value: Mostly cloudy · 50% chance of showers · high 84

facts.label: Last date
facts.value: The park lists no other Moss Meander after this one

body.text: The park's own description of the Moss Meander starts with fairies, which is where most of us left the subject. The walk picks it back up. An Ijams Park naturalist leads two hours at Mead's Quarry on how to identify different species of moss and on what moss is doing for the forest it grows in, which is more than its size suggests.

Saturday's forecast is mostly cloudy with a 50 percent chance of showers, and for this one program damp is the better condition: moss is at its greenest wet. Fifteen dollars, ages sixteen and up, registration required. Park in the quarry lot and meet staff near the picnic tables. The event page marks Saturday as the last available date.

stories.label: Ijams Park
stories.title: Songbirds get their leg bands at Mead's Quarry on Sunday, the last banding morning listed
stories.deck: The Ijams Park community science team catches, measures, bands and releases songbirds in front of whoever shows up. Five dollars puts you at the table, and the ticket covers parking.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $5 · parking included, so don't pay at the lot

facts.label: Finding it
facts.value: Staff in the gravel lot walk you to the station, about five minutes

body.text: Bird banding is the rare science you can watch from three feet away. On Sunday morning the Ijams Park community science team works its banding station near Mead's Quarry, where migratory and resident songbirds are safely caught, measured, fitted with a numbered leg band and let go. The numbers feed a long record of how the birds around the park are doing. The event page lists Sunday as the last available date.

It costs five dollars, and the ticket includes parking, so skip the pay station. Meet at the Mead's Quarry gravel lot, where a staff member walks the group to the station. Sunday is the wet day of the weekend, with showers likely and a 70 percent chance of rain, so check the event page before you drive over.

stories.title: Frogs and toads take over Saturday storytime at the Nature Playscape
stories.deck: The free Saturday storytime in the woods by Mead's Quarry is about amphibians this week. Two hours of picture books read aloud and the run of the Playscape, and it costs nothing.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Ijams Nature Playscape, Grayson Subaru Preserve · 3518 Island Home Ave

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: Free · parking $5 a car, free for members

facts.label: The book
facts.value: "Frogs and Toads," and others like it

facts.label: Bring
facts.value: A blanket or chair, a snack

body.text: Every Saturday from ten to noon, volunteer storytellers read out loud in the woods at the Nature Playscape by Mead's Quarry, and it costs nothing. This week's theme is frogs and toads. The reading list starts with a book called "Frogs and Toads" and goes on from there, and the Playscape has enough damp corners that a child who listens closely has a fair chance of meeting the subject afterward.

The format is loose. Some weeks there is a hands-on activity, and some weeks the reading is the activity and the rest is roaming. Bring a blanket or a chair and a snack. Parking at the quarry lot is $5 a car unless you are a member. Saturday has a 50 percent chance of showers, so look at the sky before you go. Next Saturday's theme is flowers and plants.

stories.label: Ijams Park
stories.title: Kids study fall wildflowers and make flower art at Ijams Park on Saturday morning
stories.deck: The Wonder of Wildflowers is built for ages six to twelve: how a flower is put together, how pollination works, what people once used each plant for, and an art piece to carry home.

facts.label: The series
facts.value: Ecosystem Explorers · come to one or come to all

facts.label: Scouts
facts.value: Fits the Junior Girl Scout Flowers badge

facts.label: For grown-ups
facts.value: The adult Fall Wildflower Walk runs the same hour · $15 · ages 14+

body.text: The park's Ecosystem Explorers series is a run of short outdoor programs for children, and Saturday's is about fall wildflowers. Ijams Park naturalists take the group through flower anatomy and the pollination process, teach how to identify the native wildflowers they come across, and explain the historical, medicinal and cultural uses of each one. It ends with every child making a flower-inspired art piece.

It is designed for ages six to twelve, the child's ticket is ten dollars, and the adult who comes along gets in free. There is no commitment to the rest of the series. The park notes it suits Junior Girl Scouts working on the Flowers badge. For a household with older kids, the adult Fall Wildflower Walk goes out at the same hour, 9:30, for fifteen dollars.

stories.title: A sound bath with gongs and singing bowls fills the Visitor Center on Sunday morning
stories.deck: KB Sound Healing plays Tibetan and crystal singing bowls and a gong for an hour while you lie still. It is indoors, which on a Sunday with rain likely makes it the sure thing.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: The large room, Ijams Park Visitor Center · 2915 Island Home Ave

facts.label: Bring
facts.value: A mat, a blanket, a pillow or a bolster

body.text: A sound bath asks nothing of you but lying down. For an hour on Sunday morning, KB Sound Healing fills the large room at the Ijams Park Visitor Center with Tibetan singing bowls, crystal singing bowls and a gong, and the people on the floor let it go past. The park describes the point as quieting the mind and letting go of the week.

Bring whatever makes a floor comfortable: a mat, a blanket, a pillow or a bolster. Twenty-five dollars, ten to eleven. Sunday's forecast has showers likely and a 70 percent chance of rain, and this is the one program on the park's Sunday that was always going to be under a roof.

stories.title: Self Care Sunday yoga meets on the Visitor Center patio, and moves inside if it rains
stories.deck: Hope Irwin's weekly hour at Ijams Park works flexibility, strength and balance for every level, kids included. With showers likely this Sunday, the class has a roof to go to.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Back patio, Ijams Park Visitor Center · 2915 Island Home Ave

body.text: Self Care Sunday is a weekly yoga class at Ijams Park taught by Hope Irwin, an hour on the back patio of the Visitor Center that mixes Vinyasa, Hatha and Power flows to work flexibility, strength and balance. All ages and all levels are welcome, and the pricing says so: ten dollars for adults, five for kids five to twelve.

Bring your own mat. Sunday's forecast has showers likely, and the park's plan for that is simple: the class moves inside. It starts at 11:30, half an hour after the sound bath in the same building lets out, for anyone who wants to make a morning of it.

stories.label: Ijams Park
stories.title: Circles with Dizzy spins hoops in the Miller Building on Thursday evening
stories.deck: The weekly adult hooping class at Ijams Park breaks each trick into its parts and rebuilds it at the room's pace. Hoops to borrow, no experience needed, and it is indoors on an 89-degree day.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Miller Education Building, Ijams Park · Island Home Ave

facts.label: Bring
facts.value: Your own hoop if you have one; a few are there to share

body.text: Dizzy teaches hooping every Thursday at six in the Miller Education Building at Ijams Park. The class takes a trick, breaks it into its base parts, drills the parts and builds up to the harder variations, at the pace of whoever is in the room. It is an adult class, no background required, and there are a few hoops to share if you don't own one.

Twenty-five dollars a workshop, six to seven. Thursday is sunny with a high near 89, the warmest day of the weekend, and this is the one thing on the park's Thursday with a roof over it. The event page has directions to the Miller Building. The class runs again October 8 and 15.
